questions.q: Why does an LLM-based app need a full input/output log, beyond just an error log, according to this lesson?
options: Because the same prompt can return a different response every time, so the only way to debug a bad answer is to see exactly what was sent and returned
Because LLM calls are deterministic and errors are the only useful thing to capture
Because error logs already contain the full prompt and response automatically
Because regulations require every app to log nothing at all
questions.explain: Unlike deterministic code, the same input can produce a different output, so inspecting the actual call is often the only way to debug it after the fact.

questions.q: What is the risk of logging every request and response body in full by default, as most LLM observability SDKs do out of the box?
options: There is no risk — logging everything in full is always the safest choice
The log store can quietly become the most sensitive database in the stack, since prompts and responses often carry PII or proprietary content
Full logging makes debugging impossible
Full logging is required by every AI regulation
questions.explain: Prompts and responses can carry sensitive customer or proprietary data, so a convenient default can turn into an unintended sensitive-data store.

questions.q: What did the four logging modes shown in this lesson (Normal, Omit Request, Omit Response, Omit Both) actually let a team do?
options: Delete all historical logs permanently with one click
Automatically translate prompts into another language before logging
Choose, per endpoint, whether to keep full detail or strip the request/response body while still logging the call happened
Block all AI calls from being logged entirely
questions.explain: The modes let a team keep full detail where it's safe and drop the sensitive body where it isn't, applied per endpoint rather than globally.

questions.q: When a request's body is omitted from logging, what still remains observable, per the screenshot in this lesson?
options: Nothing at all remains visible once the body is omitted
Only the user's full name remains visible
The omitted body is still visible to anyone with the request URL
Status, model, latency, and cost keep being tracked even though the prompt and response text are dropped
questions.explain: Omitting the body doesn't mean losing all observability — operational metrics continue to flow independently of the logged text.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a log is only useful at production volume if it can be filtered?
options: A production app can generate millions of calls a month, so an unfilterable log makes it nearly impossible to find the one call a user is asking about
Filtering is only useful for logs with fewer than ten entries total
Logs are automatically sorted by relevance with no filtering needed
Filtering removes the need to ever log requests in the first place
questions.explain: At real production scale, finding one specific call inside millions of logged requests requires being able to filter by fields like status, user, or model.
